title: Owning vs. renting
description: A plain-English look at how paying rent compares with buying a house from us using owner financing.

paragraphs: Renting and owning are both ways to have a roof. They are not the same kind of deal, and one is not automatically the smarter choice. Here is how we talk about the difference when someone sits down with us.

sections.heading: What renting is
paragraphs: When you rent, you pay for time in a place someone else owns. The payment can change when a lease comes up for renewal. When you move out, that money stays behind as rent. The landlord usually handles the bigger repairs, and the landlord also makes the rules about how long you can stay.

sections.heading: What buying from us is
paragraphs: When you buy a house from Rooted Path Homes, you are purchasing that house with owner financing, also called seller financing. We are the seller, and we are the ones you pay each month. A bank is not in the middle of the house payment.

The purchase price, the down payment, the monthly payment, and the length of the note are written down for that one house. On our homes the note usually runs somewhere between 15 and 30 years. The exact numbers are not the same for every house, and we do not publish a number until it is real. If a page says TBD, we have not set it yet.

sections.heading: The part people feel day to day
paragraphs: Owning means the house is yours to care for. A dripping faucet, a tired roof, the yard in July — those become your jobs once you buy, unless the paperwork for that house says something different. We will be straight about condition before you sign. Please don't skip the tour.

We will also walk through who pays the property taxes and the insurance, and what happens if a payment is missed. Those answers live in the note for that house. We would rather read them with you than leave them as a surprise.

sections.heading: What we will not tell you
paragraphs: We will not say that owning is always cheaper than renting. Some months it is. Some months a repair makes it not. We will not say that everyone who asks is approved. And we will not say this is the right move if you already know you need to leave town next spring. If a short stay is the real plan, renting can be the wiser choice. Tell us the truth about your timeline. We can take it.

title: How owner financing works
description: What a seller-financed note is, what we agree on before anyone signs, and the questions worth asking.

paragraphs: Owner financing and seller financing mean the same thing at our company. You buy the house from us. You pay us. We hold the note. There is no bank loan in the middle of that payment.

sections.heading: The note is the deal
paragraphs: A note is a written promise to pay. It names the house, the purchase price, the down payment, the amount due each month, and how many years the payments run. It also says what happens if a payment is late. Handshake memories fade. The paper is what we both go back to.
We agree on those terms before anyone signs. If we cannot agree, there is no deal, and that is a fine outcome. We would rather part as neighbors than force a number that only works on a good month.

sections.heading: What we look at
paragraphs: We look at each person and each house. A website form is a way to start the conversation. It is not an approval, it does not reserve the house, and it does not lock a payment. We will never promise on a web page that you are approved.

sections.heading: Questions worth asking out loud
list: When is the deed in my name?
What happens if I miss a payment?
Who pays the taxes and the insurance, and are they inside the monthly payment or on top of it?
What stays with the house — the stove, the shed, the window that sticks?
Can I read the papers at home, or show them to a lawyer or a HUD-approved housing counselor?
paragraphs: Please ask all of those. Take the papers home. A second set of eyes is a good idea, not an insult. We will answer for the house in front of us. We will not answer with a guess that is supposed to cover every house we ever sell.

sections.heading: A simple path
paragraphs: Find a home you love. Take a tour. Sit down with us to go over the terms. Get your keys. The longer version of those steps, and a renting-versus-owning comparison, is on our How It Works page.

title: What to have ready before you apply
description: You don't need a perfect file. You do need honest numbers and a few questions.

paragraphs: You do not need a binder, a perfect credit file, or the right words to call us. You do need to be straight about money and time. Here is what helps the first conversation.

sections.heading: Bring these
list: A phone number and an email you actually check.
The down payment you can really bring. If you are not sure, say you are not sure.
A monthly number you can still pay in a tight month, after groceries, the electric bill, gas to get to work, and a small surprise.
When you would like to move, even if the answer is “just looking.”
Your questions. Write them down so they don't disappear at the door.

sections.heading: Leave these at home
paragraphs: Don't stretch the numbers to impress us. A payment that only works on your best month is a bad deal for you, and it is a bad deal for us too. We would rather hear the smaller, true number.

Don't wait until you understand every word in a note. That is our job to explain, and yours to ask about until it makes sense. If a house page says TBD, the blank is not a trick. It means we have not posted that fact yet. Ask anyway.

sections.heading: At the tour
paragraphs: Walk every room. Open a closet. Look at the ceiling for stains. Step into the yard. Bring another person if you want — two sets of ears catch more than one. We will tell you what we know about the house. Please tell us what you notice.

When you are ready, the “I'm interested / apply” form on a home's page asks for your name, phone, email, the down payment you have, the monthly budget that feels comfortable, and your move timeline. Sending it starts a conversation. It does not approve you, and it does not hold the house.
